the sūtra simply states "pure awakening" (淨覺),
and awakening is precisely *vitarka* (尋).
How can it be said that one should speak of *vitarka* and *vicāra*?
Thus we know the tradition is erroneous. Question: Even if it were exclusively *vipaśyanā*, would *vipaśyanā* not then be *vitarka*?
Investigating the cause of this statement:
why did the later masters not cite it as proof? Answer: The constituent factor of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) has two aspects:
first, it is common to all schools and to the causes and fruits of both vehicles.
Furthermore, regarding the stage of subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) which is the cause of the Mahāyāna,
its essence consists solely of vitarka;

this is now correctly explained.
The two vehicles are like that.
There are two types of bodhisattvas:
those who attain sudden enlightenment, numbering either ten or four.
Because there are two different explanations regarding the first and seventh grounds,

Two tens of thousands and ten thousand [years] each constitute one person,
making forty-seven.

Twenty thousand, ten thousand, or forty-seven;
for there are two explanations within this treatise.

This applies to the coarse [stages] in this manner;
however, there are further [possibilities] regarding the subtle.

furthermore, the statement that one must sever the afflictions of cultivation in the desire realm and so forth is based on the teaching for the two vehicles and does not obstruct the turning of the mind [toward the Mahāyāna].
Although they have not yet severed the afflictions associated with desire,
they suppress these delusions and attain the fourth dhyāna;
relying on the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-samādhi), they receive a body of transformation.
Since he possesses this capacity,

Furthermore, [if one asks] why he does not attain the nine concentrations:
Because they lack the capacity to realize the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*),

and that these arise subsequently within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
That which does not appear is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, we know that both of the upper [realms] are termed "mind-made" (*manomaya*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* quotes a sūtra as saying:
Because one can enter and emerge from this meditative absorption while assuming a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) in any one of the formless realms (*ārūpya*),
it thus extends to the formless realm as well.
The Sūtra does not exclude them, as it refers to "any one" of them.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states:
"They again manifest in the realm of form."
Because it manifests only by relying upon the basis of form;
once established, it can manifest in all places,
and thus it is said that all places are included without excluding the lower three realms.
The claim by later masters that this [treatise] must necessarily arise from the three lower realms is not necessarily correct; therefore,
it was merely the Śrāmaṇera Gaṅgā who failed to understand the intended meaning.
Why is this not a sound explanation serving as valid evidence? Ximing says:

Nanda and others maintain that..."

they are called "mind-made gods" (*manomayadeva*).
This is the explanation of the Lion of the Awakened Ones (Śākyasiṃha).
The five classes of gods above the fourth dhyāna who arise from and enter the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are called the mind-made gods (*manomayadeva*).
According to those who follow the second interpretation, such as Dharmapāla, on what basis is it known that Nanda speaks of this in a general sense?
Bodhisattva Siṃhabuddhi states that only those on the five higher stages are called "mind-made gods" (*manomayadeva*).
If one follows the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*,
Bodhisattva Siṃhabuddhi provides an explanation regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) therein.
If you allow that the fourth dhyāna can arise again,
yet do not state that those in the three lower [dhyānas] are not mind-made deities (*manomayadeva*),
how can this be considered a sound explanation?

how does one explain those fifty-six passages stating that [the meditative attainments] can all manifest in every situation?
If it is claimed that "all" refers only to a partial sense, [how is this to be understood]?
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* does not employ the term "only" (*kevala*).
Regarding the teaching on the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) in the treatise,
the original text states "establishment," which signifies the sense of believing in its existence.
This is not an established meaning.
Among those of fixed nature, there are those who, being deluded regarding the Dharma, do not believe and do not enter [the path].
Those who are not deluded regarding the Dharma, though they believe in the Mahāyāna, do not take it as ultimate.
Regarding the statement that "because one believes [it] exists, one gives rise to that meditative absorption," the *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) asks:
"If one already believes in the Mahāyāna, why would it not be the ultimate?
This does not understand the intended meaning.

although one may have faith in the Mahāyāna, one does not regard it as ultimately being only a single vehicle,

Just as those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka believe that pratyekabuddhas exist,
yet do not consider the ultimate state to be exclusively that of the pratyekabuddha to the exclusion of the śrāvaka vehicle; likewise, although they believe in the greatness [of the Mahāyāna],
they lack the personal capacity to realize that greatness themselves.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that it is for the sake of those who believe in the various differences among vehicles (*yāna*) that it speaks only of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Ximing says:
"The Sūtra does not speak [of the One Vehicle] for those who do not seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."
Now, for the purpose of teaching them so that they may enter the meditative absorption of cessation, he asks them:
"Into which great teaching are they to be led?
It is by teaching the Abhidharma, the Saṃdhinirmocana, and other such works."
In none of these [earlier] teachings was it explained;
it was only in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that the six [perfections] were taught.
Furthermore, they had already been taught implicitly in the *Āgama* and other sūtras.
Therefore, one should know that "establishing" means having faith in the existence [of the object].

It is also attained in its manifest form upon being born there;

"This self-love (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*) is exclusively innate (*sahaja*)," and so forth, up to: "..."
By the power of this, ordinary beings cause the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) to continue uninterruptedly;
the same is true for noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire.
From the time of approaching death until one reaches the stage of indistinct perception,
this craving can still manifest within that interval.
Although the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that one should restrain it and not become attached, [it nonetheless arises].
It does not say "non-arising.
The Abhidharma states that it is indeed capable of subduing [the afflictions], which is not the same as non-arising.
Now, if you say "non-arising," does this not contradict [that teaching]?
One should rely on the original commentary and the Ximing (West Bright) interpretation. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, asks:
"The mind at the moment of death in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is always defiled, just like the mind at the moment of death in the existence of passing away (*cyutyabhava*)."
According to the *Vyākhyāyukti*, it is said that for one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), [the mind] is not defiled. Answer: This is also not fixed.
As it says, "like the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*");
would the mind at the moment of death-existence for a non-returner not always be defiled?
Therefore, one should simply provide a general explanation that can be further analyzed.

first, the immovable contact;
second, the contact of nothingness.
Third, there is no contact with signs.
This means that when emerging from meditative absorption, one generally emerges by means of three types of objects:

for at the time of emerging from meditative absorption,
one encounters three types of contact corresponding respectively to these three objects.
As stated in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-śrī-mūla-tantra-saṃgraha* (The Essential Summary): It is further said that for a beginner,
one enters [the attainment] by taking the cessation of feeling and perception as the object,

Because they are equally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If it were the Lord (*īśvara*),

Subsequently, whichever object it follows, it emerges;
furthermore, it has not yet attained mastery,

now, one emerges from that same meditative concentration of emptiness,
taking an existent object as the cognitive support.
